caption: At(collection, n) gives the n-th lesser twin prime, 1-indexed
KAlmostPrimes and RoughNumbers are one-parameter operators
PrimePairs(gap) selects the twin/cousin/sexy family by gap
At(collection, n) gives the n-th deficient number, 1-indexed
KFreeIntegers(k) is a one-parameter operator agreeing with SquareFreeNumbers at k=2
A list of indices selects several elements at once
A [[Range]] also works as an index list, extracting a contiguous slice
Index 0 is the collection's own head, matching Wolfram's Part[c, 0]
Several indices reach into successive levels: row 2, column 3
Negative indices work at every level
Negative indices inside an index list
A stepped [[Range]] takes every other element
Negative bounds count from the end: the last three elements
A lazy [[Range]] is indexed directly
$All$ at the first level takes a whole column
Index lists at two levels extract a submatrix (rows 1 and 3, columns 2 and 3)
A [[Span]] ($2;;4$ in Wolfram) takes a contiguous slice
A stepped [[Span]] ($1;;-1;;2$) takes every other element up to the end
A negative step ($-1;;1;;-1$) walks backwards, reversing the list
Negative bounds: the last two elements
Parts of any expression, not just lists: the second term of a sum
Reaches into a named collection, not just a literal list — here the 5th triangular number, 1-indexed
Also works on a parameterized collection like $PolygonalNumbers(k)$
At(BellNumbers, 5) is Bell(4) = 15 (1-indexed At, 0-indexed term)
Chaining $At$ reaches into nested collections, like indexing a matrix row then column
An out-of-range index evaluates to $NaN$ rather than raising an error
wolfram.note: An out-of-range index is NaN here; Wolfram leaves Part unevaluated (with a Part::partw message).
